Normalization for Multimodal Type Theory
Daniel Gratzer ORCID:0000-0003-1944-0789

Abstract
. We prove normalization for MTT , a general multimodal dependent type theory capable of expressing modal type theories for guarded recursion, internalized parametricity, and various other prototypical modal situations. We prove that deciding type checking and conversion in MTT can be reduced to deciding the equality of modalities in the underlying modal situation, immediately yielding a type checking algorithm for all instantiations of MTT in the literature. This proof uses a generalization of synthetic Tait computability —an abstract approach to gluing proofs—to account for modalities. This extension is based on MTT itself, so that this proof also constitutes a significant case study of MTT .



1.
Introduction

If type theory is classically the study of objects invariant under change of context, modal type
theory is the study of adding non-invariant connectives—
modalities
—to type theory. Given
that many natural features of particular models of type theory are not invariant under substitution,
modal type theories have sparked considerable interest. By nature, however, modal type theories must
thread the needle of presenting modalities in such a way that the classical substitution theorems of
type theory still hold.

Typically, modal type theories require modifications to the apparatus of contexts and
substitutions. Unfortunately, these tweaks are often more art than science, with expert attention
required even to make the most trivial modification to the modal structure of a type theory. In
order to address this complexity,
general
modal type theories have been
introduced
[
LSR17
,
GKNB20a
]
. These theories can be instantiated by a description of
a modal situation to produce a system enjoying the theorems usually proved by experts.

1.1.
Multimodal type theory

We focus on one such general modal type theory:
MTT

[
GKNB20a
]
.
MTT
can be
instantiated with an arbitrary collection of modalities and transformations between them to yield a
highly usable syntax. The modalities in
MTT
behave like (weak) dependent right adjoints
(DRAs)
[
BCM+20
]
so that
MTT
can be used to internalize nearly any right
adjoint. This flexibility allows
MTT
to encode calculi for guarded recursion, internalized
parametricity, and other handcrafted calculi.

More precisely,
MTT
can be instantiated by a
mode theory
, a strict 2-category describing
modes, modalities, and natural transformations between these modalities. This 2-categorical
structure is then reflected into the structure of substitutions in
MTT
, ensuring that e.g., a
transformation between two modalities
\mu
and
\nu
gives rise to a function

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}\to\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
.

While this flexibility allows
MTT
to accommodate many interesting calculi, it becomes
proportionally more challenging to prove metatheoretic results about
MTT
. In particular, the rich
substitution structure inherited from the mode theory can introduce subtle equations between
terms. The proof that the crisp induction principles can be reconstructed in
MTT

[
GKNB21
, Theorem
10.4]
, for instance, exemplifies this and hinges on many such
calculations. In fact, the metatheoretic results established by Gratzer et al.
[
GKNB20a
]

(soundness and canonicity) are results on closed terms in
MTT
, allowing their proofs to avoid the
majority of the substitution apparatus.

Crucially, it remained open whether
MTT
admitted a normalization algorithm and, consequently,
whether type checking was decidable. Even in the presence of a normalization algorithm
MTT
cannot
admit an unconditional type checking algorithm: it is not only necessary to have a decision
procedure for terms in the language, but also for modalities and 2-cells as both appear in terms for

MTT
.

In this paper we show the best possible result holds:
MTT
admits an unconditional normalization
algorithm and conversion of normal forms is decidable if conversion is decidable in the mode
theory.
1
1

1

The converse is almost, but not quite, true. Decidability of conversion for normal
forms implies that the 1- and 2-cells of the mode theory have decidable equality, as these appear
in normal forms.
As corollaries, we show that type constructors in
MTT
are always injective
and that type checking is decidable when the mode theory is decidable.
2
2

2

This requirement is potentially nontrivial e.g., the word problem for groups is known to
be undecidable and is subsumed by the problem for 2-categories.

1.2.
Normalization-by-evaluation

A normalization algorithm must begin by defining
normal forms
. Their precise formulation
depends on the situation but they always satisfy two crucial properties. First, the equality
of normal forms
u=v
is clearly decidable—often no more than structural equality—and there is
a function
\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}
decoding a normal form to a term of the same type.

Relative to a notion of normal form, a normalization algorithm sends a term
\Gamma\vdash M:A
to
a normal form
\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
such that
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}},\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}},\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}},\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}},\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
lifts to an
isomorphism between equivalence classes of terms of
A
and normal forms
[
Abe13
]
. Typically
one breaks the condition that
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}},\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}},\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}},\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-,A$}\mathclose{}{)}},\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
forms an isomorphism into three
conditions:

(1)

Completeness
: if
\Gamma\vdash M=N:A
then

\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}=\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle N,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle N,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle N,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle N,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
.

(2)

Soundness
:
\Gamma\vdash\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle M,A$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}=M:A
.

(3)

Idempotence
:
u=\mathbf{nf}_{\Gamma}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}},A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}},A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}},A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{dec}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}},A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
.

Proving normalization is an involved affair. Traditionally, one begins by fixing a strongly
normalizing confluent rewriting system presenting the equational theory of the type theory. The
normal forms are then exactly the terms of the theory which cannot be further reduced. This approach
does not scale, however, to type theories with
type-directed
equations such as the unicity
principles of dependent sums and the unit type. These equations defy attempts to present them
in a rewriting system and require type-directed algorithms.

The preeminent type-directed technique for normalization is
normalization-by-evaluation
(NbE)

[
Abe13
]
. Proving that an NbE algorithm works, however, is an extremely intricate
affair involving a variety of complex constructions. After the algorithm is defined, the proof of
correctness typically proceeds by establishing properties (1)-(3) in order. Each property, moreover,
requires a separate argument. Completeness is established through a PER model, soundness through a
cross-language logical relation, and idempotence through a final inductive argument. The first two
properties in particular are time-consuming to verify; recent work by Gratzer et
al.
[
GSB19a
]
extended NbE to a type theory with an idempotent comonad but even in this
minimal case the correctness proof occupied a 90 page technical
report
[
GSB19b
]
.

These difficulties are not unique to modal type theories, and a long line of research focuses on
taming the complexity of NbE through

gluing

[
AHS95
,
Str98
,
Fio02
,
AK16
,
Coq19
,
Ste21
]
.
This line of work recasts normalization algorithms as the construction of models of type theory in
categories defined by Artin gluing.

1.3.
Normalization-by-gluing

{exa}

Viewing objects of
\mathcal{E}
as proof-relevant predicates as described above, the exponential

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle C,\Phi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle C,\Phi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle C,\Phi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle C,\Phi$}\mathclose{}{)}}^{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle D,\Psi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle D,\Psi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle D,\Psi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle D,\Psi$}\mathclose{}{)}}}
is given by the following pair
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle C^{D},\Xi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle C^{D},\Xi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle C^{D},\Xi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle C^{D},\Xi$}\mathclose{}{)}}
where
\Xi
is
defined as follows (writing
\epsilon
for the evaluation map associated with

. See Mitchell and Scedrov

for an

Carrying out a normalization-by-gluing proof, therefore, turns the classical approach on its
head. Originally one defined the normalization algorithm then showed it to be sound, complete, and
idempotent. When carrying out the proof by gluing, the algorithm is not defined up front. Instead,
one carefully constructs a gluing category
\mathbf{Gl}(F)
built on a functor out of the category of
contexts of the initial model
\mathcal{I}
. Concretely, this is the category of syntactic contexts
and simultaneous substitutions between them up to definitional equality. The heart of the argument
then breaks down into three steps:

(1)

We show that
\mathbf{Gl}(F)
supports a particular model of type theory
\mathcal{G}
.

(2)

We define a
reify
operation which sends terms from
\mathcal{G}
to normal forms.

(3)

We show that the projection
\pi_{0}
induces a morphism of models

\mathcal{G}
\mathcal{I}
and that for a given term
x
in
\mathcal{G}
reifying
x

yields a normal form for
\pi_{0}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}
.

In particular, types in
\mathcal{G}
will be chosen such that they consist of a type from the
initial model along with a proof-relevant predicate carving out those terms which have (suitably
hereditary) normal forms. A term in this model is then a term from the syntactic model together with
a witness for the proof-relevant predicate associated with the type.

The first step and the universal property of the initial model produces a morphism of models

and the second step ensures that
\pi_{0}\circ i=\mathsf{id}
. Remarkably, this already defines a sound and complete normalization algorithm. The
algorithm simply takes a syntactic term
M:A
, regards it as an element of the initial model, and
then reifies
i\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle M$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle M$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle M$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle M$}\mathclose{}{)}}
to obtain the normal form. Moreover, because
\pi_{0}\circ i=\mathsf{id}
we
conclude that this yields a normal form for the supplied
M
.

To a coarse approximation, the construction of
\mathcal{G}
and reification specifies the
normalization algorithm and proves its soundness in a single step. The attentive reader will notice,
however, that the completeness requirement from Section
1.2
seems
to be absent from this new story. In fact, in this approach completeness is automatic and no proof
is required. Indeed, terms and types within the initial model are realized by equivalences classes
of syntactic terms and types taken up to definitional equality. Accordingly, the morphism
i
—and
therefore the normalization algorithm—cannot distinguish between definitional equal terms.

One might suspect that working with equivalence classes of terms when defining
\mathcal{G}
simply
causes the burden to shift so that—while there is no need to prove completeness separately—the
work of such a proof is spread throughout the construction of
\mathcal{G}
. In fact the opposite is
the case: working with terms up to definitional equality substantially simplifies the construction
of
\mathcal{G}
. Connectives in type theory only have universal properties up to definitional
equality. Only when working with equivalences classes therefore, can we use these universal
properties and benefit from existing results. For instance, we shall see that our construction of
dependent products in our gluing model is essentially mechanical.

The gluing approach yields other unexpected advantages. Recall that
\mathbf{Gl}(F)
intuitively consists of

proof-relevant
predicates. This proof relevance is crucial to an elegant treatement of
universes in the model
[
Coq19
]
. We are able to define the predicate associated with an
element of a universe to consist not only of an appropriate normal form but to also contain the data
of the type it encodes within the model. In proof-irrelevant settings, universes were a frequent
source of difficulty which necessitated laborious techniques to encode
[
All87
]
.

1.4.
Synthetic Tait computability

Using gluing to prove normalization is certainly an improvement over ‘free-hand’ proofs of
normalization-by-evaluation, but the picture is not as rosy as it may first appear. Models of type
theory are subject to a variety of strict equations (see Item
3
) which often
force external constructions, where naturality obligations can be prohibitive. Worse, the passage
between mathematics internal to the gluing category and external constructions is difficult
and the boundary frequently raises mismatches.

We follow Sterling and Harper
[
SH21
]
and adopt a synthetic approach to
gluing. We begin with two crucial observations. First, while models of type theory are strangely
behaved objects, one can often embed a model into a presheaf topos and thereby work in an extremely
rich setting. Second, when gluing together presheaf topoi along a nice functor

, the result is another presheaf topos and the internal language
of this topos contains lex idempotent monads (
\textnormal{$\fullmoon$},\textnormal{$\newmoon$}
) allowing one to recover both

\mathbf{PSh}(\mathcal{C})
and
\mathbf{PSh}(\mathcal{D})
.

Sterling and collaborators have then shown that it is possible to work exclusively within the
internal language of
\mathbf{Gl}(F)
to construct the normalization model and have termed this approach

synthetic Tait computability (STC)
. Experience has shown that working internally simplifies
constructions involved in the gluing model, making it practical to prove metatheorems for even
extremely complex type theories like cubical type
theory
[
SH21
,
SA21
,
Ste21
,
GB22
,
SH22
]
.

Proofs using STC construct the model within
\mathbf{Gl}(F)
by defining a sequence of constants within the
internal language. Accordingly, the heart of the normalization proof is realized by a series of
programming exercises in extensional type theory. This alone does not remove the strict equations
that cause trouble with typical gluing proofs but it does provide a systematic approach to handling
them. Concretely, within an STC proof, all the required strict equations have a particular form: for
some type operator in the object theory, we are given an element
\mathsf{op}:\textnormal{$\fullmoon$}\mathsf{Ty}

corresponding to the operator in the syntactic model, and we must extend this to an element of

\mathsf{Ty}
. Within the internal language, the two components of this problem (the element of
\mathsf{Ty}

and the proof that it extends
\mathsf{op}
) can be represented by an element of the following
dependent sum:
3
3

3

Here we have used standard syntactic sugar to represent the monadic
operations of
\fullmoon
.

\textstyle\sum_{A:\mathsf{Ty}}x\leftarrow\mathsf{op};\textnormal{$\fullmoon$}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A=x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A=x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A=x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A=x$}\mathclose{}{)}}

The second component in particular represents the aforementioned strict equation. In practice, it
is easy to obtain an element of
\mathsf{Ty}
which extends
\mathsf{op}
up to isomorphism i.e. an
element of the following type:

\textstyle\sum_{A:\mathsf{Ty}}x\leftarrow\mathsf{op};\textnormal{$\fullmoon$}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{Tm}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle Remarkably, this proves to be enough. The internal language of
\mathbf{Gl}(F)
supports a strictification
axiom
[
OP18
]
which provides a section to the canonical projection from the first type to
the second. We are therefore able to construct various connectives which agree only up to
isomorphism with their syntactic counterparts and correct them to construct the model. For instance,
a dependent product is determined by a universal property and it is possible to construct a type in

\mathbf{Gl}(F)
with this property by virtue of general categorical theorems. However, the result will only
satisfy the required equation up to isomorphism. The strictification axiom allows STC proofs to
benefit from the general categorical result without resorting to unfolding the construction supplied
by the abstract argument.

1.4.1.
Synthetic Tait computability for
MTT

Unlike Martin-Löf type theory or cubical type theory, a model of
MTT
is not a single category
equipped with additional structure. Rather, a model is a network of categories, each supporting
their own individual model of type theory which are then connected by various adjoints and natural
transformations. The internal language of any of these categories is insufficient to construct the
gluing model, so it is necessary to generalize from working in the extensional type theory of a
topos to working in all topoi simultaneously using extensional
MTT
. Each topos then comes
equipped with the structure of STC: a pair of lex monads and a strictification axiom. We prove that
this mode-local structure is respected by the
MTT
modalities between topoi and call the resulting
language
multimodal synthetic Tait computability
. The smooth interaction between MTT
modalities and the lex monads
\fullmoon
and
\newmoon
ensures that the key techniques of STC proofs
can be generalized to multimodal STC.

With this machinery, we are able to give a concise and conceptual construction of the gluing model
and extract the first normalization algorithm for multimodal type theory. In practice, this internal
proof is necessary; removing the simplifying assumption on substitutions used in the canonicity
proof given by Gratzer et al.
[
GKNB21
]
is already nearly intractable.

1.5.
Contributions

We contribute a normalization algorithm for
MTT
equipped with the full suite of connectives:
dependent sums, products, booleans, intensional identity types, a universe, and modal types. In
addition to the usual corollaries of normalization (decidability of type checking, injectivity of
type constructors, etc.), this sharpens the canonicity result of Gratzer et
al.
[
GKNB20a
]
. This algorithm applies to any choice of mode theory and therefore
simultaneously establishes normalization results for many specialized modal calculi.

In order to prove this result, we advance modern gluing techniques to apply to modal type theories
and demonstrate that extensional
MTT
itself is a suitable metalanguage for carrying out the proof
of normalization-by-gluing. We further argue that these techniques scale by extending the proof to a
version of
MTT
supplemented with crisp induction principles and deduce that e.g., normalization
continues to hold.

Section
2
gives a brief tutorial on
MTT
and introduces normal forms for this type
theory. In Section
3
, we discuss the models of
MTT
and relax the definition of a
model of
MTT
to obtain
MTT
cosmoi
. We prove that the syntactic cosmos enjoys a
privileged position among
MTT
cosmoi
(Theorem
5
). Section
4
introduces
multimodal
synthetic Tait computability
and shows that gluing together a network of topoi results in a model
of extensional
MTT
equipped with STC structure in each mode
(Theorem
18
). Finally, in Section
5
we
construct the normalization cosmos (Theorem
26
) and extract the
normalization function in Section
6

(Theorem
30
). Section
7
discusses an extension of
this proof to support crisp induction.

2.
A primer on
MTT

We collect the key ideas of
MTT

[
GKNB21
]
. First, as mentioned in
Section
1
,
MTT
is parametrized by a mode theory: a strict 2-category
\mathcal{M}

whose objects are modes, morphisms are modalities, and 2-cells are natural transformations between
modalities. Henceforth, we will work with
MTT
over a fixed mode theory
\mathcal{M}
.

MTT
plays two distinct roles in this paper. First, it is the object theory under consideration
and the subject of our normalization theorem. However, as the proof of normalization uses
MTT
as
an internal language to construct the normalization model
MTT
is also used as a metalanguage.
These two different uses invite two very distinct perspectives on the type theory. In order to
crystallize
MTT
precisely enough for the normalization result, we will view
MTT
as a
particular generalized algebraic theory (GAT). Accordingly, binding is handled by De Bruijn indices
and the theory uses explicit substitutions
[
ML92
]
. On the other hand, we will not
use De Brujin indices and explicit substitutions when working with
MTT
as a metalanguage. In
these instances, we will treat
MTT
as a normal type theory and avail ourselves of conveniences
similar to what a proof assistant like Agda might provide.

As a compromise, we introduce
MTT
in Sections
2.1
and

2.2
as a formal theory but go through several important constructions in
Section
2.3
using the informal surface-language employed by much of
Section
5
. For a comprehensive account of both perspectives, we refer
the reader to Gratzer et al.
[
GKNB21
]
.

2.1.
Mode-local connectives in
MTT

Each mode in
MTT
constitutes its own separate type theory. In fact, each mode
m
is equipped
with its own copy the of judgments of type theory e.g.,
\Gamma\ \mathsf{cx}{}\mathop{@}m
,
\Gamma\vdash A{}\mathop{@}{m}
,

\Gamma\vdash M:A{}\mathop{@}m
. Much of the theory of
MTT
is
mode-local
and only mentions a single copy of
these judgments at a time. For these connectives the rules are precisely the standard rules from

MLTT
, replicated for each mode. The connectives of type theory—dependent sums, intensional
identity types, booleans—are all incorporated in this fashion. Each mode also contains a

weak
universe à la Tarski. Explicitly, this means that there are separate codes and an

\mathsf{El}(-)
operation decoding a code to a type, but the decoding operation only commutes with
connectives up to isomorphism. While the restriction to weak universes is not fundamental, it
simplifies the proof and recent implementations have shown them to be practical
[
Red20
]
.

2.2.
Modalities in
MTT

The novelty of
MTT
comes from those connectives which mix two modes: the modalities.
MTT

draws inspiration from Fitch-style type theories
[
Clo18
,
BCM+20
]
and
defines each modality together with an adjoint action on contexts. Accordingly, each

}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu_{1}\circ\nu_{1}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{}\mathop{@}o}

Figure 1.
Key rules for contexts and substitutions in
MTT

Two basic questions remain: what is the elimination principle for
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
and which terms can
be constructed in the context
\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
? Both of these problems are addressed through the
same idea, the final component of
MTT
. We generalize the context extension
\Gamma.A

from
MLTT
to annotate each variable with a modality:

\frac{\Gamma\ \mathsf{cx}{}\mathop{@}m\quad\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}\vdash A{}\mathop{@}{n}}{\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}\ \mathsf{cx}{}\mathop{@}m}

Intuitively,
\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
plays the same role as
\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
and comes
equipped with a similar universal property: a substitution
\Delta\vdash\gamma:\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{}\mathop{@}m

is precisely determined by a substitution
\Delta\vdash\gamma^{\prime}:\Gamma{}\mathop{@}m
and a term

\Delta.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}\vdash M:A\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\gamma^{\prime}.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\gamma^{\prime}.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\gamma^{\prime}.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\gamma^{\prime}.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{}\mathop{@}n
. The ordinary context extension
\Gamma.A

is recovered by taking
\mu=\mathsf{id}
; the equation
\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{id}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{id}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{id}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{id}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}=\Gamma
ensures
that the universal properties of
\Gamma.A
and
\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{id}\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{id}\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{id}\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{id}\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
match.

Despite the similarities between
\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
and
\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{id}\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{id}\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{id}\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{id}\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
, they
occupy different positions in the theory. The variable rule of
MTT
is adjusted to take into
account modal annotations and require that the modalities in the context must cancel a variable’s
annotation:

\frac{\Gamma\ \mathsf{cx}{}\mathop{@}m\quad\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}\vdash A{}\mathop{@}{n}}{\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid As in Martin-Löf type theory, it is necessary to apply a weakening substitution

to

when describing the type of
\mathbf{v}_{0}
. The normal variable rule arises again as a special case after

. Note that attempting to state such a variable rule for

\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{id}\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{id}\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{id}\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{id}\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
would quickly introduce issues around substitution within the

Remark 1
.

From the view of Fitch-style type theories where
-.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
is left adjoint to the modal type,
this rule plays the role of the counit; it allows us to pass from

to
A
.

The addition of modal annotations creates a redundancy in our system: we may hypothesize of

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}

Remark 2
.

Fitch-style type theories require

\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\nu\circ\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\nu\circ\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\nu\circ\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\nu\circ\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}\vdash{{\uparrow}}.{\mathsf{mod}_{\mu}(\mathbf{v}_{0})}:\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\nu\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\nu\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\nu\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\nu\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{}\mathop{@}o

to be invertible. Such an inverse, however, again disrupts substitution in the presence of
multiple modalities. For an extended discussion of this point and various potential solutions, see
Gratzer et al.
[
GCK+22
]
.

In addition to modal types, dependent products in
MTT
are also modalized so that
A\to B
is
replaced by
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}\to B
:

\frac{\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}\vdash M:B{}\mathop{@}m}{\Gamma\vdash\lambda\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle M$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle M$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle M$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle M$}\mathclose{}{)}}:\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}\to B{}\mathop{@}m}\frac{\Gamma\vdash M:\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{)}}\to B{}\mathop{@}m\quad\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}\vdash N:A{}\mathop{@}n}{\Gamma\vdash M\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle N$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle N$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle N$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle N$}\mathclose{}{)}}:B\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\mathsf{id}}.{N}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathsf{id}}.{N}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\mathsf{id}}.{N}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{id}}.{N}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{}\mathop{@}m}

This feature is a useful convenience; it ensures that many functions avoid the need to accept an
argument of modal type only to immediately apply the elimination rule. We will see frequent examples
of this pattern later as
MTT
is used as a metalanguage.

2.3.
Standard combinators within
MTT

As the assignment
\Gamma\mapsto\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
is pseudofunctorial, its adjoint action on types is
likewise functorial
up to propositional equality
. In particular, there are equivalences

\mathsf{triv}:\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{id}\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{id}\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{id}\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{id}\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}\to A
and

\mathsf{comp}:\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}\to\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\circ\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\circ\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\circ\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\circ\nu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
:

\displaystyle\mathsf{triv}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}=\mathsf{let}_{\mathsf{id}}\ \mathsf{mod}_{\mathsf{id}}(y)\leftarrow x\ \mathsf{in}\ y

\displaystyle\mathsf{triv}^{-1}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}=\mathsf{mod}_{\mathsf{id}}(x)

\displaystyle\mathsf{comp}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}=\mathsf{let}_{\mathsf{id}}\ \mathsf{mod}_{\mu}(y_{0})\leftarrow x\ \mathsf{in}\ \mathsf{let}_{\mu}\ \mathsf{mod}_{\nu}(y_{1})\leftarrow y_{0}\ \mathsf{in}\ \mathsf{mod}_{\mu\circ\nu}(y_{1})

\displaystyle\mathsf{comp}^{-1}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{)}}=\mathsf{let}_{\mathsf{id}}\ \mathsf{mod}_{\mu\circ\nu}(y)\leftarrow x\ \mathsf{in}\ \mathsf{mod}_{\mu}(\mathsf{mod}_{\nu}(y))

Each modality
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
also satisfying the modal principle referred to as
axiom K

i.e., they preserve finite products. In practice, this property serves as an internalization of
functoriality as it provides a canonical comparison map

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A\to B$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A\to B$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A\to B$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A\to B$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}\to\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}\to\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid B$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid B$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid B$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid B$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}

in order to avoid needing to immediately eliminate

2.4.
Normal and neutral forms in
MTT

As mentioned in Section
1.2
, the starting point for normalization
is the definition of normal form. In
MTT
—as in other type theories—normal forms are presented
together with a class of neutral forms. Intuitively, normal forms capture terms in
\beta
-normal
and
\eta
-long form while neutrals are chains of eliminations applied to a variable.

We define normal and neutral forms as separate syntactic classes, equipped with their own family of
typing judgments and decoding functions sending them to terms. Dependency complicates this
definition as various typing rules require substitution in the types of premises or the
conclusion. Unfortunately, it is just as hard to define substitution on normal forms as it is to
define normalization in general
[
WCPW04
]
. Accordingly, a normal form (resp. neutral,
normal type) is typed by the judgment
\Gamma\vdash^{\!\!\raisebox{0.0pt}{\tiny$\mathsf{nf}$}}u:A{}\mathop{@}m
(resp.
\Gamma\vdash^{\!\!\raisebox{0.0pt}{\tiny$\mathsf{ne}$}}e:A{}\mathop{@}m
,
\Gamma\vdash^{\!\!\raisebox{0.0pt}{\tiny$\mathsf{nf}$}}\tau{}\mathop{@}m
) where
A

is not required to be any sort of normal form. Furthermore, these judgments are defined
inductive-recursively with decoding functions
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\displaystyle u$}\mathclose{}{|}}{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\textstyle u$}\mathclose{}{|}}{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\scriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{|}}{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{|}}
(resp.
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\displaystyle e$}\mathclose{}{|}}{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\textstyle e$}\mathclose{}{|}}{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\scriptstyle e$}\mathclose{}{|}}{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle e$}\mathclose{}{|}}
,
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\displaystyle\tau$}\mathclose{}{|}}{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\textstyle\tau$}\mathclose{}{|}}{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\tau$}\mathclose{}{|}}{\mathopen{}{|}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\tau$}\mathclose{}{|}}
)
which send a normal form (resp. neutral, normal type) to its corresponding piece of syntax. Normal
and neutral forms for mode-local connectives are unchanged from their standard presentation in type
theory:

(Normals)

u

\Coloneqq

\lambda\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\;\mid\;}{}{\mathsf{up}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle e$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle e$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle e$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle e$}\mathclose{}{)}}}{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\;\mid\;}{}\mathsf{mod}_{\mu}(u){\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\;\mid\;}\dots

(Neutral)

e

\Coloneqq

\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\alpha}{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\;\mid\;}{}e\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle u$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\;\mid\;}{}\mathsf{letmod}(\mu;\nu;\tau;e;u){\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\;\mid\;}\dots

(Normal types)

\tau

\Coloneqq

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid\tau$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid\tau$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid\tau$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid\tau$}\mathclose{}{)}}\to\sigma{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\;\mid\;}{}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid\tau$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid\tau$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid\tau$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid\tau$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\;\mid\;}{}\mathsf{El}(u){\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\;\mid\;}\dots

We defer a more complete presentation of the judgments and decoding function to
Figure
3
, but remark that the neutral form for variables is
annotated with a 2-cell and index, decoding to
\mathbf{v}_{0}
together with a combination of weakening
and 2-cell substitutions
{\uparrow}
and
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
. Note that we require that
\mathsf{El}(-)
commute
with type formers only up to isomorphism (weak Tarski universes) we must include neutral and normal
forms for e.g.,
\mathsf{El}(\widehat{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}})
as well as other type connectives. We include only those for

\widehat{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}}
as they are representative of the general pattern.

Definition of selected normals, neutrals, and normal types

To ensure that normal forms are
\eta
-long, neutrals can only be ‘injected’ into normals by

{\mathsf{up}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{)}}}
for types without an
\eta
law e.g., at modal types but not at dependent
products. Finally, we emphasize that normal forms are freely generated so their equality is
decidable if equality of modalities and 2-cells is decidable. There is some more subtle than it may
appear as normal forms are indexed by arbitrary types—which are not freely generated. This can be
overcome by an argument given by Altenkirch and Kaposi
[
AK17
]
which gives a

bidirectional
algorithm for deciding the equality normal forms, neutrals, and normal form
types. Note that this argument, in turn, relies on the injectivity of various type constructors
which we will prove only in Section
6.2

Renamings

While normal and neutral forms are not stable under substitution, they are stable under the
restricted class of
renamings
. The formal definition of renamings is presented in
Figure
2
. Intuitively, they are the smallest class of substitutions closed
under weakening, composition, identity, modal substitutions (
-.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
,
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
), and
extension by variables
\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\alpha}
.

Renamings are easily seen to act on normal forms, neutral forms, and normal types. Unlike normals
and neutrals, however, renamings are taken up to a definitional equality which ensures that e.g.,
composition is associative and that modal substitutions organize into a 2-functor. This poses no
issue as the action of renamings on normals and neutrals send definitionally equal renamings to
identical normals and neutrals, ensuring that the action lifts to equivalences classes.

A nontrivial definitional equality on renamings is essential, however, as it ensures that the class
of contexts of mode
m
and renamings between them organizes into a category
\mathsf{Ren}_{m}
and that the
assignments
m\mapsto\mathsf{Ren}_{m}
,
\mu\mapsto-.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
, and
\alpha\mapsto\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\alpha$}\mathclose{}{\}}}

define a 2-functor
{\mathcal{M}}^{\mathsf{coop}}
\mathbf{Cat}
.

3.
Models and cosmoi

Gratzer et al.
[
GKNB21
]
introduced
MTT
as a generalized algebraic theory
so that
MTT
is automatically equipped with a category of models. A standard result of GATs
ensures that the syntax of
MTT
organizes into an initial model which opens the possibility
of semantic methods for proving results about syntax. Gratzer et al.
[
GKNB21
]

then repackages the definition of models in the language of natural models
[
Awo18
]
.

3.1.
Natural models of
MTT

MTT
given by Gratzer et
al.
[
GKNB21
]

(1)

Diagram

takes advantage of the model of extensional
MLTT
in a
presheaf topos
[
Hof97
]
and we have written
\tau_{m}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}
to denote the

. We refer to a

(3)

Unlike dependent sums or products, modal types do not have a universal property—an
\eta
law—so
they cannot be encoded by a single pullback. Instead we must describe the elimination principle
separately. Following Gratzer et al.
[
GKNB21
]
, we encode the elimination
principle as an internal lifting structure.

{defiC}

[Definition 18
[
Awo18
]
]
An internal lifting structure

As models of a particular GAT, models of
MTT
assemble into a category. A morphism between models

F
and
G
is given by a 2-natural transformation
F
G
along with natural assignments of
terms and types of
F
to the terms and types of
G
. All of these operations are required to
strictly preserve term, type, and context formers. We refer the reader to
Gratzer et al.
[
GKNB21
]
for a precise description.

Finally, a standard result of GATs is that the
syntactic model
occupies a distinguished place
in the category of models:

Theorem 4
.

Syntax is the initial model of
MTT
.

3.2.
MTT
cosmoi

As mentioned in Section
1
, normalization is proven through the construction of a model of

MTT
together with a map from this model to syntax. Models of
MTT
and morphisms
between them are difficult to construct, however, because of the extreme strictness of morphisms and
the requirement that each
\tau_{m}
be a representable natural transformation. Prior to
normalization, therefore, we introduce a weakened notion of model: an
MTT
cosmos. An
MTT

cosmos is an axiomatization of a natural model of
MTT
, but rather than working in presheaf topoi
and requiring that
\tau_{m}
is a representable natural transformation a cosmos requires only that

\tau_{m}
be a morphism in a locally cartesian closed category equipped with structure such as
Diagrams
2
and
3
.

.

A morphism of
MTT
cosmoi is both more and less restrictive than a morphism of
MTT

models. While a morphism of models need not induce an LCC functor between the relevant presheaf
categories, a morphism of cosmoi is not required to strictly preserve context extension or the
choice of terminal context. It so happens that the only map of consequence in this paper is locally
cartesian closed, so the additional structure of morphisms of cosmoi poses no issue. Not requiring
the strict preservation of context extension and dropping the representability requirements from

MTT
cosmoi, however, ensures that cosmoi are far easier to construct.

Remark 6
.

While we have proven this result quite generally, we will apply it only in the special case
where
\pi
is a 2-natural transformation between strict 2-functors and required isomorphisms of
left adjoints are likewise identities. The reader may accordingly safely ignore these coherences
when reading the proof without consequence.

Remark 7
.

Both Theorem
4
and
5
are categorical
abstractions of
rule induction
. Indeed,
4
is used to prove

5
—via the construction of an appropriate displayed
model
[
KKA19
]
—and the latter takes the place of rule induction in the proof of
normalization (see Theorem
30
).

Proof 3.1
.

We write
\mathbf{El}_{m}
,
\mathbf{Ty}_{m}
and
\mathbf{Tm}_{m}
instead of
\tau_{m}
,
\mathcal{T}_{m}
, and
\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{m}
in the syntactic
model, reserving the latter exclusively for
G
. We write
\llbracket\mu\rrbracket
for the functor sending

\Gamma
to
\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
. We begin by replacing
G
by an equivalent strict 2-functor so that

\pi
becomes strictly 2-natural.

We construct a displayed model of
MTT

[
KKA19
]
which lies over the syntactic
model. Using the existing coherence result for
MTT

[
GKNB20b
]
, we only
ensure that
\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\nu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\nu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\nu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\nu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
and
\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\circ\nu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\circ\nu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\circ\nu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\circ\nu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}

Modal types

Suppose we are given a context
(X,\Gamma,\alpha)
and a type
(\bar{A},A)
in the context

(G(\mu)_{{!}}(\mu)(X),\Gamma.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{\}}},\gamma\circ\llbracket\mu\rrbracket^{*}(\alpha)\circ\beta_{\mu})
. Writing
\bar{B}
for the transpose of
\bar{A}
, we form the modal type as

(\mathbf{Mod}_{\mu}(\bar{B}),\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}})

It remains to check that these types are coherent i.e.:

\pi(\mathbf{Mod}_{\mu}({\bar{B}}))=\mathchoice{\left\lfloor\mkern-2.0mu{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}}\mkern-2.0mu\right\rfloor}{\left\lfloor\mkern-2.0mu{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}}\mkern-2.0mu\right\rfloor}{\lfloor\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}\rfloor}{\lfloor\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid A$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}\rfloor}\circ\alpha

By assumption,
\pi(\bar{B})=\mathchoice{\left\lfloor\mkern-2.0mu{A}\mkern-2.0mu\right\rfloor}{\left\lfloor\mkern-2.0mu{A}\mkern-2.0mu\right\rfloor}{\lfloor A\rfloor}{\lfloor A\rfloor}\circ\gamma\circ\llbracket\mu\rrbracket^{*}(\alpha)\circ\beta
. By
our assumption that
\pi
satisfies Beck-Chevalley

\pi(\bar{B})=\widehat{\mathchoice{\left\lfloor\mkern-2.0mu{A}\mkern-2.0mu\right\rfloor}{\left\lfloor\mkern-2.0mu{A}\mkern-2.0mu\right\rfloor}{\lfloor A\rfloor}{\lfloor A\rfloor}\circ\gamma}\circ\alpha
. The result follows from
the fact that
\pi
preserves
\mathbf{Mod}_{\mu}
.

3.3.
Presheaf cosmoi

Example
3.2
shows that each model of
MTT
induces an
MTT
cosmos. In
fact, such cosmoi are particularly well-behaved as they are comprised of presheaf topoi connected by
adjoint triples. These cosmoi enjoy a privileged role in our proof and we observe some of their
unique behavior.

{defi}

A presheaf cosmos
F
is a cosmos where
F
is a strict 2-functor, each
F\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle m$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle m$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle m$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle m$}\mathclose{}{)}}
is a presheaf
topos, and each right adjoint
F\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{)}}
sends small families to small families.

What distinguishes presheaf cosmoi from other cosmoi is the rich internal language they
offer. Gratzer et al.
[
GKNB21
]
have proven that such a cosmos
F
supports a
model of
extensional

MTT
with the same mode theory where
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
is interpreted by

F\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu$}\mathclose{}{)}}
. We will now use extensional
MTT
as a
multimodal metalanguage
to specify the
structure of an
MTT
cosmos as a sequence of constants, thereby reducing its construction to a
series of programming exercises. It is this characterization of
MTT
-cosmoi that we will
use in Section
5
to construct the normalization cosmos.

Remark 8
.

Some caution is required here, as a presheaf cosmos will frequently host more than one
interpretation of
MTT
. A presheaf cosmos is always equipped with this modal metalanguage
(extensional
MTT
) which can then be used to specify a model of (intensional)
MTT
. This is
comparable to Diagram
1
, where type theory is used to describe a model of
type theory.

\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\to\mathsf{Tm}_{m}(A(\mathsf{true}))\to\mathsf{Tm}_{m}(A(\mathsf{false}))\to(b:\mathsf{Tm}_{m}(\mathsf{Bool}))\to\mathsf{Tm}_{m}(A(b))

\displaystyle\_

4.

In light of Section
3

Section

{exa}

Intuitively
\mathbf{Gl}(\rho)
is a category of proof-relevant
\mathcal{F}
-predicates on
\rho
-elements of

\mathcal{E}
. To cultivate this intuition, consider
\mathcal{F}=\mathbf{Set}
and
\rho=\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1},-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1},-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1},-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1},-$}\mathclose{}{]}}
. An
object of
\mathbf{Gl}(\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1},-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1},-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1},-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1},-$}\mathclose{}{]}})
is a triple of
(S,E,f)
which induces a proof-relevant
predicate
\Phi(e)=f^{-1}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle e$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle e$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle e$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle e$}\mathclose{}{)}}
on the global points of
E
. Following Tait
[
Tai67
]
, we
refer to elements in the image of
f
as
computable elements
.
Morphisms are then morphisms of
\mathcal{E}
equipped with additional structure ensuring that
computable elements are sent to computable elements.

We now reap the first reward from considering proof-
relevant
predicates:
\mathbf{Gl}(\rho)
is
extremely well-behaved.

{thmC}
[
[
AGV72
,
CJ95
]
]

\mathbf{Gl}(\rho)
is a presheaf topos and
\pi_{0}
is a logical functor with left and right adjoints.

As a presheaf topos,
\mathbf{Gl}(\rho)
enjoys a model of extensional type theory with a strictly
cumulative hierarchy of universes and a universe of propositions
\Omega
. We can use this language
to
synthetically
build logical relations models
[
SH21
]
. In order to
effectively construct such models, however, we must supplement type theory with primitives specific
to
\mathbf{Gl}(\rho)
. The most fundamental of these is a proposition:

{defi}

The
syntactic proposition

\mathbf{syn}:\Omega
is interpreted in
\mathbf{Gl}(\rho)
as the subterminal
object
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}},\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{F}},{!}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}},\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{F}},{!}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}},\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{F}},{!}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}},\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{F}},{!}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
.

Recalling the correspondence between objects of
\mathbf{Gl}(\rho)
and predicates,
\mathbf{syn}
is the predicate
on
\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}}
with no computable elements. What makes this proposition useful is its ability to
wipe out the obligation to track computable elements. A morphism

More intuitively, realignment states that a predicate lying over an object in
\mathcal{E}
can be shifted
to lie over an isomorphic object. A proper motivation of realignment is deferred to its use in
Section
5
, but broadly realignment will be used to satisfy the strict
equalities demanded by Definition
3.2
where a priori two constants might agree only up to
isomorphism.

Theorem 8.4 of Orton and Pitts
[
OP18
]
shows that a Hofmann–Streicher universe satisfies realignment for
levelwise decidable propositions. Using the presentation of
\mathbf{Gl}(\rho)
as a presheaf
topos
[
CJ95
]
,
\mathbf{syn}
is clearly levelwise decidable and so realignment at
\mathbf{syn}
is
constructively valid.

{defi}

The language of synthetic Tait computability is extensional type theory with a cumulative
hierarchy of universes and a universe of propositions equipped with a distinguished proposition

\mathbf{syn}:\Omega
such that each universe satisfies the realignment axiom for
\mathbf{syn}
.

This subsection is summarized by the following result, which might be termed the ‘fundamental lemma’
of STC:

Theorem 10
.

\mathbf{Gl}(\rho)
is a model of STC.

Remark 16
.

Technically,
\mathbf{syn}
,
\fullmoon
, and
\newmoon
should be always annotated with a mode. In light of
these results, however, we shall omit this annotation and systematically
identify

\mathbf{syn}_{m}

and
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mu\mid\mathbf{syn}_{n}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\mu\mid\mathbf{syn}_{n}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mu\mid\mathbf{syn}_{n}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mu\mid\mathbf{syn}_{n}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
. As both are subterminal, there are no coherence issues in this
identification.

Remark 19

One may explicitly present
\mathbf{Gl}(\mathbf{i}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle m$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle m$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle m$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle m$}\mathclose{}{]}}^{*})

\mathsf{Cx}_{m}

[
CJ95
]
. This is a category whose objects are given by the
disjoint union of

5.1.
Prerequisites for the normalization cosmos

Before we extend
\mathcal{G}
to an
MTT
cosmos, we import features of
\mathcal{G}
into the
language of MSTC to specialize the latter to this situation. In this section, we begin using the
interpretation of
MTT
to work internally to
\mathcal{G}
and explicitly record the extensions to
MSTC required for the normalization proof.

{nota}

[Dependent open modality]
As
\textnormal{$\fullmoon$}A=\mathbf{syn}\to A
, we will write
\textnormal{$\fullmoon$}_{z}A\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle z$}\mathclose{}{)}}=\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle z:\mathbf{syn}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle z:\mathbf{syn}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle z:\mathbf{syn}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle z:\mathbf{syn}$}\mathclose{}{)}}\to A\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle z$}\mathclose{}{)}}
for the

Following Hofmann
[
Hof99
]
, the constructors for normal forms, neutrals, and normal types
lift can be realized in
\mathbf{PSh}(\mathsf{Ren}_{-})
by a form of higher-order abstract syntax. As

\mathsf{Nf}_{m}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
,
\mathsf{Ne}_{m}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
, and
\mathsf{NfTy}_{m}
lie over
\mathsf{Tm}_{m}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
and
\mathsf{Ty}_{m}
, one can
extend this higher-order abstract syntax presentation to
\mathcal{G}
and realize each normal form,
neutral, and normal type as a constant of
\mathsf{Nf}_{m}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
,
\mathsf{Ne}_{m}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}
, or
\mathsf{NfTy}_{m}
which
collapses to the appropriate syntactic constant under
z:\mathbf{syn}
. As a simple example, the normal
form type for booleans along with the ordinary boolean type former induce maps
